title: You Can Always Give Them Five More Minutes
author: The Daily Dad
summary: This Daily Dad reflection uses the story of David Reed Gamboa Brandhorst, a young child killed alongside his two fathers when their flight was hijacked on September 11, 2001, to make an argument about the unrecognized 'last times' embedded in ordinary parenting. Its structure moves from the family's final ordinary afternoon at a West Hollywood playground, where David asked for 'just five more minutes' and his fathers granted it as they always did, to a broader claim that every parent lives inside a series of unmarked final moments — a last diaper change, a last ride, a last hug — most of which end naturally but some of which end suddenly and unjustly. The piece's practical argument is narrow and direct: because none of these endings announce themselves in advance, parents should default toward granting a child's small requests for more time and attention, since doing so is simultaneously a gift to the child and to the parent's own future memory. It closes by quoting the memorial inscription now standing at the playground where David played, folding his family's private loss into the shared public memory of the 25th anniversary of September 11.
points: The essay centers on David Reed Gamboa Brandhorst, a young boy killed with his two fathers when their flight from Boston to Los Angeles was hijacked and crashed into the World Trade Center's south tower on 9/11.
Its narrative hinge is a mundane final exchange at a playground -- David asking for 'just five more minutes, Daddy' and his fathers granting it, not knowing it would be the last time.

The piece generalizes this into a claim that all parents live among unrecognized 'last times' (a last diaper change, a last stroller ride, a last hug), most ending ordinarily but some ending suddenly and unfairly.

Its practical takeaway is that because these endings never announce themselves, parents should default toward granting children's requests for a little more time, since doing so serves the parent's own memory as much as the child's wish.

The piece closes by quoting the actual memorial inscription for David now standing at the West Hollywood park where he played, tying his family's private loss to the public 25th-anniversary remembrance of 9/11.
quotes: After a wonderful afternoon on the playground, they told David it was time to go and he shouted back, "Just five more minutes, Daddy." And they relented as they always did. They just didn't know it was the last time.

There's a last time you change a diaper. There's a last time you get to speak with them. There's a last time you push them in a stroller or walk them to school or drive them to their summer job. There's a last meal, a last hug.

The reason it surprises us is that we don't know when...and because we love them, we love life so much, it always comes too soon. Which is why, when our kids ask for a few more minutes, for one more hug, for a ride, for anything, we should find a way to give it to them.

David's boundless energy and love were a gift to his Papa and Daddy and all those who knew him. David loved to play at this park-a little boy racing to climb and swing under the watchful eyes of his Papa and Daddy.

May David's playground always be a place of joy, laughter and safe haven for every little boy and girl who asks for just one more trip down the big slide-or as David would say, "Just five more minutes, Daddy.
